lines: Notice the two failure modes on the left: crash at the worst possible hour, or quietly lose a field forever and never know it happened.
The stream on the right didn't avoid the problem. It was configured, ahead of time, to handle exactly this.
Before I answer, think about what goes wrong without this property. A restart sees the same file list it saw five minutes ago. Nothing in that list has changed.
What has to exist somewhere so the stream knows it already dealt with this?
answer: A durable memory — something that survives the restart itself, not just something held in a variable while the stream was running.
That's the whole job of a checkpoint. It isn't about speed. It's about the stream remembering its own history across a crash.

lines: Resist the urge to call one of these the upgrade and the other the legacy option. They have different costs, and one of those costs changes with scale.
Listing gets more expensive as the number of files grows. Notification doesn't — but it asks for more permission up front.
Watch the second run closely. It's handed the exact same two files from before, plus one real newcomer. Only the newcomer gets through.
This isn't a claim about what should happen. It's the same checkpoint object, called twice, actually enforcing it.
Don't rank these top to bottom — notice what each one is willing to give up. One gives up a moment of availability. One gives up ever stopping. One gives up nothing except your patience.
Picking the wrong one for your situation isn't a small mistake — it's building the exact failure mode you were trying to avoid.
Here's the part worth sitting with: this isn't a trash bin. It's a structured record — the field, and exactly which file it came from.
Which means recovering it later isn't digging through logs. It's just a query.
Notice what this doesn't need: no checkpoint to manage, no schema evolution to configure, no always-on process sitting and waiting.
For the job it's built for, that's not a weaker tool. It's the right amount of machinery.
If you only remember one line: discovery mode is a cost decision, and schema-evolution mode is a failure-shape decision — two separate choices, not one knob.
And nothing that doesn't match the schema has to be silently gone. It just has to be looked at.
Before I answer, notice what's absent from this job: no surprise columns expected, no files arriving unpredictably, no reason for anything to be always running.
Does that job actually need everything Auto Loader builds in?
answer: No. A stable, periodic, predictable load is exactly the case the lighter tool was built for.
Reaching for the heavier machinery here wouldn't make the pipeline safer — it would just be machinery nobody needed.
